claims.claim_text: Wallach documents that specific mineral deficiencies produced specific deficiency diseases in distinct geographic regions — each disease appeared wherever the local soil lacked that mineral. His examples: iodine deficiency caused goiter (a swollen thyroid) in communities far from the sea; selenium deficiency caused Keshan disease, a cardiomyopathy (disease of the heart muscle), in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency caused pica (a compulsive craving to eat non-food substances) in South Africa; and copper deficiency caused enzootic ataxia (a copper-deficiency disorder of movement and coordination) in Australia. In his words: "Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia) was common in Australia, etc."
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's health framework is built on an unusually large base of comparative pathology. As a pathologist for a multi-institution research program - The Center for the Biology of Natural Systems, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) along with several zoos and universities - he performed autopsies on a scale almost no one else has: more than 20,000 of them, spanning over 17,500 captive wild, laboratory, and domestic animals across more than 454 species, plus 3,000 humans for comparison. That vast cross-species record is what led him to his central claim - that creatures dying of so-called "natural causes" were really dying of nutritional deficiency diseases. In his words: "As a comparative pathologist, I (Wallach) performed more than 20,000 autopsies of over 17,500 captive wild animals, laboratory species and domestic animals, of over 454 species and 3,000 humans for a comparison."
claims.verbatim:
As a comparative pathologist, I (Wallach) performed
more than 20,000 autopsies of over 17,500 captive wild
animals, laboratory species and domestic animals, of over 454
species and 3,000 humans for a comparison.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's stance on carbohydrates and sugars: they are not essential nutrients. His reasoning is that the body can make all the carbohydrate and sugar it needs - for energy, upkeep, and structural repair - by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins inside the cell, so none has to come from the diet. This runs counter to the popular view of carbohydrates as a required food group. In his words: "Contrary to popular belief, carbohydrates and sugars are not essential nutrients by anybody's standards, as we can make all of the carbohydrates and sugars we need for energy and maintenance and repair of structural components by breaking down and reconfiguring fats and proteins at the cellular level."
claims.verbatim:
Contrary to popular belief, carbohydrates and sugars
are not essential nutrients by anybody’s standards, as we
can make all of the carbohydrates and sugars we need for
energy and maintenance and repair of structural components
by breaking down and reconfiguring fats and proteins at the
cellular level.

claims.claim_text: Wallach counts 12 essential amino acids - the protein building blocks the body cannot make for itself and so must obtain from food: valine, tyrosine, tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, histidine, phenylalanine, arginine, taurine, and leucine. (Mainstream nutrition usually lists nine; Wallach's list adds tyrosine, arginine, taurine, and histidine.) He warns that if any essential amino acid is missing from the diet for any length of time, a specific - sometimes reversible - deficiency disease results. A footnote adds that selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer considered selenomethionine (the selenium form of methionine) a 13th essential amino acid. In his words: "There are 12 amino acids that are required by the body as protein building blocks, and because the body is unable to manufacture them, they are termed 'essential amino acids.'"
claims.verbatim:
There are 12 amino acids that are required by the body
as protein building blocks, and because the body is unable to
manufacture them, they are termed “essential amino acids.”

claims.claim_text: For more than 65 years it was known that omega-3 essential fatty acids were needed to prevent disease - but because the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had ruled the evidence "inconclusive," it was actually illegal to tell people that omega-3 supplements could lower their risk of stroke and sudden cardiac death. Wallach fought this: his company (Wellness Lifestyles, Inc.) petitioned the FDA for a qualified health claim, and after a hard-fought battle, won - on September 8, 2004 the FDA allowed the claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk (Docket No. 03Q-0401). In his words: "To make a long story short, Wellness Lifestyles, Inc (Wallach) filed a petition for an Amended Health Claim: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Coronary Heart Disease (Co-Petitioner); Docket No. 03Q-0401; filed on 6/23/2003; qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004."

To make a long story short, Wellness Lifestyles,
Inc (Wallach) filed a petition for an Amended Health
Claim: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Coronary Heart Disease
(Co-Petitioner); Docket No. 03Q-0401; filed on 6/23/2003;
qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004.

claims.claim_text: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is no - he calls it an essential nutrient. He points out that cholesterol is a necessary building block of the structural membranes of every cell, of all steroid hormones, and of the brain's myelin (the fatty insulating sheath around nerves) and nerve cells themselves. This counters the popular view of cholesterol as merely something to avoid. In his words: "Cholesterol is an essential nutrient and an essential component of the structural membranes of all cells, all steroid hormones and is a major component of brain (myelin) and nerve cells."
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential nutrient and an essential
component of the structural membranes of all cells, all steroid
hormones and is a major component of brain (myelin) and
nerve cells.

claims.claim_text: Wallach warns that vitamin deficiencies during pregnancy can cause catastrophic birth defects - he lists neural tube defects, intellectual disability, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft lip, cleft palate, and heart defects among the possible outcomes. This is a general warning; the specific nutrient-to-defect links (such as folic acid and neural tube defects, or zinc and cleft palate) are covered as their own operational claims. In his words: "Deficiencies of many vitamins during pregnancy can result in catastrophic birth defects (neural tube defects, mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft lip, cleft palate, heart defects, etc.)."
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of many vitamins during pregnancy
can result in catastrophic birth defects (neural tube defects,
mental retardation, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cleft
lip, cleft palate, heart defects, etc.).

claims.claim_text: Wallach attributes the "morning sickness" of early pregnancy to a deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): he notes it is commonly seen in the first trimester and is thought to be caused by too little B6. This complements his morning-sickness protocol elsewhere, which treats it with B6 plus a B-complex. In his words: '"Morning sickness" commonly observed in the first trimester of pregnancy is thought to be due to pyridoxine deficiency.'
claims.verbatim:
“Morning sickness” commonly observed in the first
trimester of pregnancy is thought to be due to pyridoxine
deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Does the birth-control pill deplete a nutrient? Per Wallach, yes: 15 to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives show symptoms of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency - including malaise, depression, and glucose intolerance (trouble regulating blood sugar). In his words: "Fifteen to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives show the symptoms of pyridoxine deficiency manifested by malaise, depression and glucose intolerance."
claims.verbatim:
Fifteen to 20 percent of women taking oral contraceptives
show the symptoms of pyridoxine deficiency manifested by
malaise, depression and glucose intolerance.

claims.claim_text: Wallach corrects even Linus Pauling - the two-time Nobel laureate - on minerals. Pauling (author of The Nature of the Chemical Bond) treated minerals as secondary to vitamins, recommending only eight to eleven of them at minimal doses. His selenium advice is Wallach's example of how wrong this was: Pauling insisted selenium's safe upper limit was just 15 mcg, whereas today the recommended safe limit is 200 to 1,000 mcg for an adult. In his words: "Linus Pauling, two time Nobel laureate, and author of the great work, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, relegated minerals to secondary importance to vitamins, recommending only eight to eleven minerals (calcium, magnesium, phosphorous, iron, zinc, copper, manganese, chromium, molybdenum, iodine and selenium) and then only at minimal doses - an example was selenium for which he insisted the upper safe limit was 15 mcg (today the recommended safe limit for selenium is 200 to 1,000 mcg for an adult)."
claims.verbatim:
Linus Pauling, two time Nobel laureate, and author of the
great work, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, relegated minerals
to secondary importance to vitamins, recommending only eight
to eleven minerals (calcium, magnesium, phosphorous, iron,
zinc, copper, manganese, chromium, molybdenum, iodine and
selenium) and then only at minimal doses - an example was
selenium for which he insisted the upper safe limit was 15 mcg
(today the recommended safe limit for selenium is 200 to 1,000
mcg for an adult).

claims.claim_text: Wallach links selenium deficiency to prostate cancer - and uses Pauling himself as the example: Pauling, who downplayed minerals, died of prostate cancer at age 94, which Wallach attributes to a selenium deficiency (selenium is strongly prostate-protective in his framework). In his words: "Pauling died of prostate cancer at age 94 - a common result of a selenium deficiency."
claims.verbatim:
Pauling died of prostate cancer at age 94 - a
common result of a selenium deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Wallach reframes obesity as a mineral-deficiency disease - "not a disease of excess." His evidence: a study in the Journal of the American Medical Association (December 15, 2004) found that the longer immigrants live in the US, the more likely they are to be obese, averaging about a 10-pound weight gain after 15 years. He calls this the "Feedlot Syndrome" - people placed on the mineral-depleted American "four food group" diet, having lost their traditional mineral-rich "culinary" and garden ashes, gain weight unless they consciously supplement with plant minerals. In his words: '“The longer you live in America, the more likely you are to be obese.” (Remember - obesity is a mineral deficiency disease - not a disease of excess)'
claims.verbatim:
“The longer you live in America,
the more likely you are to be obese.” (Remember - obesity is a
mineral deficiency disease - not a disease of excess)

claims.claim_text: A central Wallach teaching: our food has been massively depleted of vitamins and minerals as farm soils were stripped. A USDA database comparing common foods between 1975 and 2004 shows dramatic losses - for example, broccoli lost 54% of its calcium and 74% of its vitamin A, onions lost 95% of their vitamin A, apples lost 60% of their iron, and kale lost 46% of its calcium. His conclusion: we can no longer get adequate minerals from food alone and must supplement, especially with plant-derived minerals (the "culinary ashes" of traditional diets). In his words: "Only when one looks at a USDA data base that compares the level of vitamins and minerals in certain common foods between 1975 and 2004, do we truly understand how depleted our foods have become since we gave up the back yard gardens and wood ashes (plant minerals)."
claims.verbatim:
Only when one looks at a USDA data base that
compares the level of vitamins and minerals in certain common
foods between 1975 and 2004, do we truly understand how
depleted our foods have become since we gave up the back
yard gardens and wood ashes (plant minerals).

claims.claim_text: How many minerals does the body actually need? Wallach's starting point: more than 79 elements and minerals have been detected in human and animal tissue, and simply being present in the tissue meets the first criterion for calling a substance an 'essential nutrient.' From there, he says thousands of studies support designating 60 of those 79 as truly essential - the mineral backbone of his '90 essential nutrients' framework (60 minerals, 16 vitamins, 12 amino acids, and 3 essential fatty acids). In his words: "More than 79 elements and minerals have been detected in animal and human tissue (i.e. - blood, liver, muscle, brain, bones, connective tissue, etc.) in the 20th and 21st centuries. Their presence in human tissue fulfills the first criteria for designating an element or mineral an 'essential nutrient.' Literally thousands of additional studies provide support for designating 60 of these 79 elemental nutrients to be essential nutrients."
claims.verbatim:
More than 79 elements and minerals have been detected
in animal and human tissue (i.e. - blood, liver, muscle, brain,
bones, connective tissue, etc.) in the 20th and 21st centuries. Their
presence in human tissue fulfills the first criteria for designating
an element or mineral an “essential nutrient.” Literally thousands
of additional studies provide support for designating 60 of these
79 elemental nutrients to be essential nutrients.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's rule of thumb for how much a single missing mineral can cost you: on average about ten different deficiency diseases can arise from the absence of any one essential mineral - and calcium is his extreme case, capable of producing as many as 147 different diseases when the body is short of it. In his words: "On the average there are ten deficiency diseases that can occur in the absence of each essential mineral, others, like calcium can produce as many as 147 different diseases when the body is deficient."
claims.verbatim:
On the average there are ten deficiency diseases that
can occur in the absence of each essential mineral, others, like
calcium can produce as many as 147 different diseases when
the body is deficient.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes cravings - pica (a compulsive craving for non-food items) and 'the munchies' - as the body's earliest warning sign of trace-mineral deficiency, and stresses that at this early stage it is fully reversible: restore the missing minerals and the cravings disappear. In his words: "Pica, or the 'munchies' appear in a mild form in this early stage of deficiency. This phase of trace mineral deficiency returns to normal (including the elimination of the 'munchies') quickly following the return of an optimal intake."
claims.verbatim:
Pica, or the “munchies” appear in a mild form

claims.claim_text: Wallach maps trace-mineral deficiency as a four-stage progression that mostly hides from standard testing until it is advanced. Initial Depletion - the body quietly adjusts and tests still look normal; the only clue is 'lack of energy' plus mild cravings. Compensated Metabolic - specific biochemical functions falter (low blood sugar, irregular heartbeat, loss of hair color, mild weight gain) and cravings intensify into 'chocoholic' or 'cola addict' behavior. Decompensated - serious metabolic, cognitive, emotional, developmental and structural disorders appear. Clinical - full disease and even death; yet orthodox physicians rarely diagnose the mineral cause, and the cure is often simply replacing the specific missing element. In his words: "Initial depletion of trace elements in animals and humans is characterized by changes only in the metabolism of the element itself in response to a suboptimal intake, the individual target tissue compensating so that no disturbance of biological structure or function are detectable by means of a test. However, the individual usually complains of 'lack of energy.'"

Initial depletion of trace elements in animals and
humans is characterized by changes only in the metabolism
of the element itself in response to a suboptimal intake, the
individual target tissue compensating so that no disturbance
of biological structure or function are detectable by means of
a test. However, the individual usually complains of “lack of

energy.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach ties trace-mineral deficiency to a broad spectrum of cognitive and emotional/behavioral problems - not just physical disease. On the cognitive side he lists learning disabilities, ADD, ADHD and autism; on the emotional side, depression, manic depression/bipolar, anxiety and panic attacks - extending at the extreme to explosive anger and the volatile 'Jekyll-and-Hyde' or 'bad seed' temperament he attributes to a mineral-starved nervous system. His point for the reader: mood and behavior problems many people never connect to nutrition may trace back to a correctable deficiency. In his words: "...the metabolic (i.e. - pre-diabetes, significant weight gain, obesity), cognitive (i.e. - learning disabilities, ADD, ADHD, autism, etc.), emotional (i.e. - DR. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde, 'Bad Seeds,' depression, manic depression, bipolar...)"

The decompensated phase of trace element deficiency is
characterized by the appearance of serious clinical symptoms

“Bad Seeds,” depression, manic depression, bipolar

claims.claim_text: Left uncorrected, Wallach says trace-mineral deficiency finally reaches a 'clinical' stage of full-blown disease and even death - he lists cardiomyopathy (heart-muscle disease), diabetes, aneurysm (a bulging, weakened artery wall), arthritis, periodontal (gum) disease, degenerative disc disease, cataracts, goiter (a swollen thyroid) and morbid obesity among the endpoints. His hopeful counterpoint: orthodox physicians almost never trace these back to a missing mineral, yet the cure is often as simple as replacing the specific trace element. In his words: "The clinical phase of trace mineral deficiency is characterized by the onset of full blown disease states and even death (i.e. - cardiomyopathy, diabetes, aneurysm, arthritis, periodontal disease, degenerative disc disease, cataracts, goiter, morbid obesity, etc.). For most trace mineral deficiencies in the clinical phase, correct diagnosis by the 'orthodox' physician is almost nonexistent; the cure, however, is accomplished simply by the replacement of the specific trace element."

The clinical phase of trace mineral deficiency is
characterized by the onset of full blown disease states and

cataracts, goiter, morbid obesity, etc.). For most trace

claims.claim_text: For searchers looking for Wallach's position: among the developmental problems he attributes to nutritional deficiency during fetal development, he lists sexual orientation - 'gay orientation' - alongside dyslexia, spina bifida, neural tube defects, cleft lip and palate, heart defects, cerebral palsy and Down syndrome. Consistent with his other writing, he frames it as a preventable congenital event tied to maternal nutritional deficiency rather than a lifestyle choice. Presented faithfully and neutrally as his view. In his words: "developmental (i.e. - dyslexia, gay orientation, spina bifida, neural tube defects, cleft lip, cleft palate, heart defects, cerebral palsy, Downs Syndrome, etc.)"

claims.claim_text: Are common calcium pills a good deal? Wallach says no - metallic mineral supplements like calcium carbonate are barely absorbed (about 8-12% in the young, falling to 3-5% after age 35-40). Worked example: a 1,000mg calcium carbonate tablet is only 400mg of actual (elemental) calcium, and at roughly a 10% absorption rate you net just ~80mg usable - so to truly get 2,000mg of usable calcium you'd have to swallow about 25 tablets a day (a 100-count bottle would last only 4 days). In his words: "Two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules or tablets do not give you 2,000 mg of calcium - they only supply 800 mg of elemental calcium and at a 10% availability rate you will net only 80 mg of available calcium. Therefore, to get 2,000 mg of usable calcium from a 1,000 mg capsule or tablet of calcium carbonate, you would have to take 25 capsules each day!"
claims.verbatim:
Two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules or tablets do not
give you 2,000 mg of calcium - they only supply 800 mg of
elemental calcium and at a 10% availability rate you will net
only 80 mg of available calcium. Therefore, to get 2,000 mg of
usable calcium from a 1,000 mg capsule or tablet of calcium
carbonate, you would have to take 25 capsules each day!

claims.claim_text: How much real (elemental) calcium a supplement delivers depends heavily on its form. Wallach's table for the metallic calcium in a 1,000mg tablet: calcium gluconate 90mg, calcium carbonate 400mg, calcium acetate 230mg, calcium citrate 210mg, calcium lactate 140mg - and cow's milk (1,000mg of fluid) just 10mg. (These are the milligrams of calcium present; how much you actually absorb is lower still - see his metallic-absorption note.) In his words: "Amounts of Metallic Calcium in a 1,000 mg Tablet - Calcium gluconate 90; Calcium carbonate 400; Calcium acetate 230; Calcium citrate 210; Calcium lactate 140; Cow's milk (1,000 mg fluid) 10"

claims.claim_text: Chelated minerals - where an amino acid, protein, or enzyme is wrapped ('claw,' from the Latin) around each mineral - absorb far better than plain metallic ones: about 40-65%, which Wallach calls a 400% improvement over metallic minerals (8-12%). He notes the form was a 1940s livestock-industry invention (the original chelating agent, calcium EDTA, was a German pre-WWI antidote for arsenic and lead exposure, still used today for intravenous chelation of clogged arteries), and that you can spot chelated forms on a label as selenomethionine, chromium picolinate, or 'amino acid chelate.' In his words: "Chelated minerals are approximately 40 to 65% bioavailable, a 400% increase over the availability of metallic minerals - certainly, a significant improvement over the amounts elemental minerals that are absorbed."
claims.verbatim:
Chelated minerals are approximately 40 to 65%
bioavailable, a 400% increase over the availability of metallic
minerals - certainly, a significant improvement over the


amounts elemental minerals that are absorbed.

claims.claim_text: What is a colloidal mineral - and what does 'nano-technology' have to do with it? Wallach describes a colloid as a substance existing as ultra-fine particles suspended in a medium, so small (about a billion would fit in a hundredth of a cubic inch) that they don't dissolve into individual atoms the way salt does. He notes colloids keep their special qualities as long as the particles stay within a size range of about 1 to 100 nanometers - a range, he points out, known as 'nano-technology.' In his words: "The interesting thing about colloids is that they remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble at different concentrations as long as a larger number if not all of the particles are within a range of sizes of colloids (1nm to 100nm) known as 'nano-technology.'"
claims.verbatim:
The interesting
thing about colloids is that they remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble at different concentrations as long as a
larger number if not all of the particles are within a range of
sizes of colloids (1nm to 100nm) known as “nano-technology.”

claims.claim_text: Why can't you just swallow ground-up rock minerals? Wallach's answer: inorganic mineral colloids are 'too large' to pass through the gut wall or cell walls into the bloodstream. But in the presence of amino acids (from protein-containing food), a small percentage of them get converted into chelated minerals and organic colloids that CAN be absorbed through the intestinal membranes - this absorbable state he calls a 'crystalloid.' He adds that almost all nutrients are actually taken up by 'active transport' (the intestinal cell reaching out with a pseudopodium, a finger-like projection, to engulf the particle), not by passively drifting through a membrane. In his words: "In the presence of amino acids, a small percentage of the inorganic colloids form chelated minerals and organic colloids which are able to be dialyzed through the mucus membranes of the intestinal walls into the blood stream - this bio-available mineral state is known as a 'crystalloid.' Crystalloids or organic colloids readily pass through cell walls, while inorganic colloids are 'too large.'"
claims.verbatim:
In the presence of amino acids, a small
percentage of the inorganic colloids form chelated minerals
and organic colloids which are able to be dialyzed through the
mucus membranes of the intestinal walls into the blood stream
- this bio-available mineral state is known as a “crystalloid.”

Crystalloids or organic colloids readily pass
through cell walls, while inorganic colloids are “too large.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach classifies colloidal minerals into four forms that differ wildly in usability: (1) unprotected 'rock flour' - bare inorganic colloids from sea beds, clays and 'glacial milk,' which are really just metallic minerals and only feed plants (and only in healthy, microbe-rich soil); (2) organic mineral colloids from living systems (bacteria, fungi, green food crops, animals, humans) coated in a water-loving substance like gelatin, albumin or collagen - a 'crystalloid' with bioavailability up to 98%; (3) a carbon-coated form (a 10-12 carbon chain), the most stable natural type; and (4) an industrial form not found in nature, made by coating metallic colloids with sulfated castor oil. The second - the plant/living organic colloid - is the highly absorbable form his framework favors. In his words: "The second type of mineral colloid is found in living systems of bacteria, fungi, green plants (food crops), animals and humans and is coated with a water-loving (hydrophilic) substance such as gelatin, albuminoids or collagen. This coating protects the now 'organic mineral colloid' and allows it to be a crystalloid for absorption, storage and physiological uses and thus maximizing its bioavailability up to 98%."

The second type of mineral colloid is found in living
systems of bacteria, fungi, green plants (food crops), animals

substance such as gelatin, albuminoids or collagen. This
coating protects the now “organic mineral colloid” and allows

claims.claim_text: Wallach counts silver as an essential mineral - not because an enzyme requires it, but because it works as a systemic disinfectant and immune-system stimulator. A silver deficiency, he says, leaves the immune system impaired (a link Dr. Robert Becker documented in The Body Electric, tying low tissue and dietary silver to higher illness rates). He puts the safe intake at up to 400 mg of silver per day. In his words: "Humans can consume 400 mg of silver per day. A silver 'deficiency' results in an impaired immune system."
claims.verbatim:
Humans can consume 400 mg of silver per day. A
silver “deficiency” results in an impaired immune system.

claims.claim_text: How does silver fight germs? Per Wallach, it acts as an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal 'anti-metabolite' - it disables the specific enzymes microbes need to breathe (respire). He notes it is such an efficient bactericide (bacteria-killer) that our great-grandmothers dropped silver dollars into fresh milk to keep it from spoiling at room temperature. In his words: "Silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-metabolite that disables specific enzymes that microorganisms use for respiration. Silver is such an efficient bactericide that our great-grandmothers put silver dollars into fresh milk to keep bacterial counts down and to keep it from spoiling at room temperature."
claims.verbatim:
Silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-metabolite that disables specific enzymes that microorganisms
use for respiration. Silver is such an efficient bactericide that
our great-grandmothers put silver dollars into fresh milk to
keep bacterial counts down and to keep it from spoiling at
room temperature.

claims.claim_text: Beyond killing germs, Wallach says silver actively drives tissue repair: it stimulates fibroblast (stem) cells to multiply faster, generating primitive, embryonic-like cells in wounds that can then differentiate into whatever cell types are needed to heal the wound or rebuild lost tissue. In his words: "Human fibroblast (stem) cells were able to multiply at a greater rate, producing large numbers of primitive, embryonic cells in wounds. These stem cells are able to differentiate into whatever cell types that are necessary to heal the wound or replace tissue mass."
claims.verbatim:
Human fibroblast (stem) cells were able to multiply at a
greater rate, producing large numbers of primitive, embryonic
cells in wounds. These stem cells are able to differentiate into
whatever cell types that are necessary to heal the wound or
replace tissue mass.

claims.claim_text: Is silver dangerous? Wallach's answer: at standard intake it is absolutely non-toxic - but chronic overdosing carries one distinctive risk, argyria: a permanent, whole-body dusky blue-gray discoloration of the skin (a 'tattoo' that does not fade). In his words: "Silver is absolutely non-toxic to humans at standard rates of consumption. CAUTION: chronic overdoses can cause a whole body tattoo that produces a permanent dusky blue discoloration of the skin."
claims.verbatim:
Silver is absolutely non-toxic to humans at standard rates of consumption. CAUTION:
chronic overdoses can cause a whole body tattoo that produces
a permanent dusky blue discoloration of the skin.

claims.claim_text: Silver has a long clinical track record that Wallach relays from the older medical literature (presented for reference, not as his own protocol). Colloidal silver was reported in the British Medical Journal (Sir Malcolm Morris, 1917) as soothing rather than irritating - subduing inflammation and promoting healing - and used for enlarged prostate with bladder irritation, pruritus (itching) of the anus, perineal eczema, and hemorrhoids; J. Mark Hovell (1917) reported benefit for the Eustachian tubes, nasal-and-throat congestion (catarrh), and mouth, throat and ear infections; and T.H. Anderson Wells (Lancet, 1918) used it intravenously for a post-childbirth blood infection. Silver sulfadiazine (Silvadene) is used in about 70% of U.S. burn centers and stops the herpes simplex virus behind cold sores. In his words: "colloidal silver is free from the drawbacks of other preparations of silver, viz. pain caused and discoloration of the skin. Instead of producing irritation, it has a distinctly soothing effect. It rapidly subdues inflammation and promotes healing of the lesions. It can be used with remarkable results in enlarged prostate with irritation of the bladder, in pruritus ani and perineal eczema, and in hemorrhoids."
claims.verbatim:
colloidal silver is free from the drawbacks of
other preparations of silver, viz. pain caused and discoloration
of the skin. Instead of producing irritation, it has a distinctly

claims.claim_text: Surprisingly, Wallach classifies aluminum as an essential nutrient - specifically the organically-bound colloidal aluminum found in all soil-grown plants, which he considers nontoxic. Its biological job: activating the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase. In animal studies, an aluminum-deficient diet produced congenital limb defects (non-genetic birth defects) in the young and liver cirrhosis (scarring) in adults, while supplementing it raised newborn survival - leading chemistry professor Gerhard Schrauzer to call it 'probably an essential mineral for human nutrition.' In his words: "Aluminum's known biological function is to activate the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase. Deficiencies of aluminum created in laboratory diets results in congenital limb defects (non-genetic birth defects) in laboratory animals and cirrhosis of the liver in mature animals."
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum’s known biological function is to activate
the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase. Deficiencies of aluminum
created in laboratory diets results in congenital limb defects
(non-genetic birth defects) in laboratory animals and cirrhosis
of the liver in mature animals.

claims.claim_text: Aluminum is everywhere in the food supply, and Wallach frames that as normal, not alarming: it is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust (about 12%) and is taken up by every plant grown in soil - so you cannot eat any grain, vegetable, fruit or nut, or drink any natural water, without ingesting it. He notes it is especially high in plankton and red algae and concentrates in mammals' hair and lungs. In his words: "Aluminum represents 12% of the earth's crust and is the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and the most abundant metal in the earth's crust."

claims.claim_text: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease? Wallach says no - and calls the scare a myth built on 'a single faulty study.' He cites the follow-up work: a 1992 study in Nature by Frank Watt and colleagues at Oxford, using a highly accurate technique, found the same aluminum levels in the brains of non-Alzheimer's controls as in Alzheimer's patients; a 1997 Berkeley newsletter and a 2007 German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment opinion both concluded there is no proven link between dietary aluminum and Alzheimer's. In his words: "A single faulty study over 35 years ago suggested a link between chronic aluminum exposure and Alzheimer's disease."

between chronic aluminum exposure and Alzheimer’s disease.
